turns.text: Hey! how performant is ray marching when representing rotating curbs with cell shading and black borders on them?...

items.text:
I'm assuming "curbs" means cubes, like the robot-core boxes. In short, ray marching is fast enough at your art resolutions, but it is the wrong tool for cubes and is always slower than what you have.

**Cost model.** The cost is pixels × march steps × primitives in the SDF (signed distance field). The figures below are estimates I worked out, not measurements from the engine. For one robot I assumed about 15 rotated boxes and about 32 steps:

| Target | Pixels | Box-SDF evals per robot | 20 robots at 60 fps |
|---|---|---|---|
| 128² pass-1 tile | 16K | ~8M | ~300 GFLOPS, which saturates the 2018 MacBook's iGPU (its integrated GPU) |
| 43² block-res tile (`ROBOT_ART`) | 1.8K | ~0.9M | ~30 GFLOPS, feasible but a real slice of the frame |

Rasterizing the same robot costs about 180 triangles, which is effectively free. Sphere tracing pays per pixel per step, whereas rasterization pays per vertex plus one cheap fragment.

**What matters for your case**
- **Marching is unnecessary for boxes.** Ray-box intersection is analytic using the slab test: one evaluation per box per pixel, with no steps. That is about 30× cheaper than marching and gives exact hard edges. Rotation means transforming the ray by the box's inverse mat3, which is cheap.
- **Silhouette outlines are easy, but the rays that draw them are the expensive ones.** The standard trick is to track the minimum distance along the ray and draw black where the ray misses but came within the outline width. Those grazing rays are the ones that run to the maximum step count. So the cost concentrates on silhouettes, and a robot is mostly silhouette at 43 texels.
- **Interior ink lines between adjacent cubes are not free.** You need a primitive-ID or normal-discontinuity compare against neighbouring pixels, which is a post pass. Your inked post pass already does exactly that on rasterized output.
- **Cel shading costs nothing either way.** It is a quantized N·L (surface normal dot light direction) in any pipeline.
- **Aliasing is a non-issue.** Hard all-or-nothing edges match the art direction, so you would skip the antialiasing work that ray marchers usually need.

**Where ray marching would pay off.** It suits shapes that triangles handle badly: smooth-min blends, rounded or melting forms, domain repetition, and cheap ambient occlusion and soft shadows. In this game that means the shoggoth, not the cube robots. It only needs one 256 px tile, so a fully marched organic boss at art resolution fits the budget. That is the same economics as DRIVE/BACKDROP, where a tiny target gets a heavy per-pixel shader and one upscaled quad.

**Recommendation.** Keep the rasterize-plus-inked-post pipeline for the cube robots. For a "pure shader" robot, use analytic ray-box rather than marching. Reserve true SDF marching for blobby things, rendered at block resolution.

turns.text: what is "analytic ray-box" ?

items.text:
"Analytic" means you solve for the hit point with a formula instead of searching for it step by step.

**Ray marching** asks the SDF "how far is the nearest surface?", moves the ray forward by that amount, and repeats. It takes roughly 10 to 60 iterations per pixel to converge on a surface. It works for any shape, but each pixel pays for a loop.

**Analytic ray-box** uses the fact that a box is simple enough for the intersection to have a closed-form answer, known as the slab method. A box is the overlap of three "slabs". Each slab is the space between two parallel planes: one pair for x, one for y, one for z. For each axis, one division gives the ray parameter `t` where the ray enters that slab and where it leaves it. The ray is inside the box only while it is inside all three slabs at once, so:

```glsl
// ray: origin ro, direction rd — box centred at origin, half-size b
vec3 t1 = (-b - ro) / rd;      // t at the 3 "min" planes
vec3 t2 = ( b - ro) / rd;      // t at the 3 "max" planes
vec3 tn = min(t1, t2);         // entry t per axis
vec3 tf = max(t1, t2);         // exit t per axis
float tNear = max(max(tn.x, tn.y), tn.z);   // inside all 3 slabs from here…
float tFar  = min(min(tf.x, tf.y), tf.z);   // …until here
bool hit = tNear < tFar && tFar > 0.0;
// hit point = ro + rd * tNear
```

This gives the exact hit distance in about a dozen arithmetic operations, with no loop, no step budget and no epsilon. It also gives the normal with no extra work: whichever axis produced `tNear` is the face that was hit, so the normal is ±that axis. Marching has to estimate the normal from 4 to 6 extra SDF samples.

**Rotated boxes.** Don't rotate the box. Transform the ray into the box's local space instead: `ro' = R⁻¹(ro - centre)`, `rd' = R⁻¹ rd`. Then run the same axis-aligned test, and rotate the normal back out afterwards. That adds one mat3 multiply per box.

**A whole robot.** Loop over its roughly 15 boxes, keep the smallest positive `tNear` along with that box's ID and normal, and cel-shade the result. That is about 15 cheap tests per pixel, against roughly 32 steps × 15 SDF evaluations when marching, and the edges come out mathematically exact.

The box ID you keep also handles the black interior lines. If a neighbouring pixel hit a different box, or hit the same box at a large depth jump, draw an ink pixel. Your inked post pass already does that kind of edge detection.

Marching is the general-purpose fallback for shapes that have no such formula, such as blends, noise-displaced surfaces and fractals. Boxes, spheres, planes, capsules and cylinders all have closed-form intersections, which is why classic ray tracers use them.

turns.text: do you think we would improve the framerate if we actually directly render the robots in 3d on the screen and don't do an intermediate buffer?...

items.text:
I don't think so. Going by the batch code in `robot-core.js`, the framerate would stay about the same or get slightly worse, and you would lose the look. I read the code but have not profiled anything.

**What the intermediate buffer costs today**

Per frame, for all robots together, the pipeline does this:

- It binds the framebuffer once and does one scissored clear, covering only the tile rows in use.
- It issues one `drawArrays` per robot (two if armed) into a 128² tile. A robot is about 15 cubes, roughly 180 triangles.
- It runs one inked post draw for the whole batch, written at block resolution. That is 43² ≈ 1.8K fragments per robot, so 20 robots come to about 37K fragments of edge-detect shader. For comparison, one full-screen Retina layer is about 5M fragments.
- It then draws one textured quad per robot through the normal batch.

So the buffer adds two framebuffer switches, one small clear and one tiny post draw per frame. Pass 1 rasterizes at most 16K pixels per robot with a trivial shader. None of that is a significant cost.

**What direct-to-screen rendering would change**

- **Draw calls stay the same.** It is still one skinned draw per robot with its 27-mat4 palette upload. That per-robot CPU and driver cost is the part that actually shows up, and removing the buffer does nothing to it.
- **Fill cost goes up.** A robot covers more screen pixels than its 128² tile once you account for Retina and zoom, and each of those pixels would run the lighting shader. Today they cost one NEAREST fetch each.
- **The main canvas would need a depth buffer.** It has none now. Every full-screen layer would pay depth bandwidth, which is the same kind of cost that made `?aa=1` drop the MacBook to 30 fps. You would also interleave depth-tested 3D draws with the 2D batch, which means more flushes and state changes.
- **The ink outlines still need a buffer.** The black borders come from a post pass that compares neighbouring pixels using the part-id stored in alpha. Without an offscreen target you would need either a full-screen post pass, which is far more expensive than 37K fragments, or inverted-hull outlines. Inverted hulls double the geometry, look different, and don't give part-to-part ink lines.
- **You lose the chunky pixel look.** Direct 3D at native resolution gives smooth HD robots with no 43-texel blocks. That is exactly what the Design section of CLAUDE.md rules out: robots have to be low-resolution baked images that then move smoothly.

**Where the robot cost probably sits**

If robots show up in a `?perf` trace, my guess is the CPU side. That means the JS pose math (`posePlan` plus the M4 matrix chains, per robot, per frame) and the 27-mat4 uniform upload per draw, not the framebuffer. The `sprites` span and the `robots` counter in the trace would confirm it. The fixes would then be:

- cheaper pose evaluation;
- skipping offscreen robots, if that isn't done already;
- not re-rendering a tile for a robot that hasn't changed, such as corpses or idle passives with a frozen pose. This is the same trick as the portrait and head bakes.

I would keep the buffer and measure before changing anything. If you send me a `?perf` dump from a crowded floor, I can tell you where the robot time actually goes.

turns.text: wait... why is robot-core.js javascript and not webgpu?....

items.text:
JavaScript versus WebGPU isn't really an either/or. JavaScript is a language and WebGPU is an API you call from JavaScript (or from wasm), so they sit on different layers.

`robot-core.js` is already GPU code. The JS only orchestrates: it computes each robot's pose matrices (`posePlan`), uploads them as uniforms, and issues one `drawArrays` per robot. The rendering work runs on the GPU in GLSL shaders: the skinned vertex shader, the lighting, and the inked and pixelated post pass. The GPU API it uses is WebGL 1 (`getContext("webgl")`, both here and in `renderer.js`).

A WebGPU version would still be a `.js` file. It would call `device.createRenderPipeline(...)` instead of `gl.drawArrays(...)`, and the shaders would be WGSL instead of GLSL. The per-frame JS work would stay the same.

So the real question is why this uses WebGL and not WebGPU. There are two reasons:

- **Reach.** WebGL 1 runs everywhere, including Safari and the 2018 MacBook you use as the performance floor. WebGPU support in Safari and Firefox is recent, Linux support is patchy, and old Intel GPUs often lack it. You would need a WebGL fallback anyway, which means maintaining two renderers.
- **One shared context.** `createRobotPipeline(gl)` runs on the same GL context as `renderer.js`, so the robot atlas is a texture the main batch samples directly. You can't mix the two APIs on one canvas or share textures between them. Moving the robots to WebGPU means porting all of `renderer.js`: about 2.7K lines, every POSTFX kind, DRIVE, BACKDROP, the pixel groups, and the static cache.

WebGPU wouldn't make this workload faster. Its wins are compute shaders, lower per-draw CPU overhead when you have thousands of draws, and storage buffers. You have about 20 to 40 robot draws per frame and tiny fragment loads, and none of that is limited by the API. If robots ever show up in `?perf`, I'd expect the cost to be in one of three places, and each has a fix that doesn't need WebGPU:

| Cost | Fix |
|---|---|
| Pose math in JS (`posePlan` and M4 chains per robot per frame) | Move it into the wasm (Rust), or cache frozen poses such as corpses and idle passives. No API change needed. |
| 27-mat4 uniform upload and one draw per robot | With WebGL **2**: put the matrices in a texture or UBO and use instancing, so all robots go in one draw call. WebGL 2 is supported everywhere that matters now. |
| Framebuffer switches and the post pass | These are already batched to one per frame, so there is nothing left to gain. |

If you ever want a more modern API here, WebGL 2 gives you instancing, UBOs, and `texelFetch` with the same context, GLSL (a `#version 300 es` port), and architecture. I wouldn't do even that before a perf trace shows robot draw overhead is an actual problem.

items.text:
I went through `_renderRobot` and the batch path. My answer is mostly no to the first question and yes to the second, but the gain from either is small.

**Would Rust/wasm be faster?**

The JS does two things per robot:

1. **Matrix math.** `posePlan` is scalar trig. After that comes about 60 `M4.mul` calls to build the 15 to 27 pose matrices. The matrices already come from a preallocated pool (`m4alloc` / `M4.reset`), so nothing is garbage collected. V8 JIT-compiles this kind of Float32Array arithmetic well. I estimate it at about 5 to 15 µs per robot. Wasm might be 1.5 to 2× faster on that part, which saves roughly 0.1 to 0.2 ms per frame with 30 robots.
2. **WebGL calls.** Each robot makes a viewport call, a scissor call, 3 uniform uploads and 1 or 2 draws. **Wasm cannot call WebGL directly.** Every `gl.*` call made from Rust goes through a JS glue function (web-sys). That makes those calls the same speed or slower, and the palette has to be copied out of wasm memory as well. This part usually costs more than the matrix math, because the browser validates each call and forwards it to the GPU process.

Porting to Rust would speed up the cheap part and add a hop to the expensive part, so it isn't worth doing. The current split is the right one: the wasm sends one command stream, and JS stays next to the GL calls.

**Could more run on the GPU?**

Yes, and the design is straightforward: move the matrix chain into the vertex shader and draw all the robots as one instanced draw.

- **`posePlan` stays on the CPU.** It is branchy scalar logic with a switch over poses, and it outputs about 12 numbers: `bob, lean, zback, legA, legB, armLp, armRp, armRaise, armOut, elbow, recoil` and the flags.
- **Those 12 scalars, plus facing, colours and the tile index, become per-instance attributes.** That replaces the 27 mat4 (432 floats) you currently upload per robot.
- **The vertex shader rebuilds the hierarchy** (root → hip → knee → shin, and so on) from the scalars. Each vertex knows its part index, so it runs only its own chain of 3 to 5 small transforms. For about 540 vertices × 30 robots that is about 16K vertices, which costs a GPU almost nothing.
- **The tile placement moves into the shader** as a clip-space offset per instance, replacing the per-robot `viewport` and `scissor` calls. The whole batch then needs one `drawArraysInstanced` call. `ANGLE_instanced_arrays` is supported everywhere on WebGL 1, so this does not need a WebGL 2 port.

Each robot would go from about 60 matrix multiplies and 7 GL calls to writing about 20 floats into a buffer. The whole batch would need one buffer upload and one draw call.

This design has three complications:

- **Held weapons.** Each weapon uses a different mesh range. You could draw one instanced batch per weapon type. Or you could bake every weapon into the merged mesh and collapse the unused boxes to zero scale, which is the trick `headless` already uses.
- **Spill between tiles.** Without a per-tile scissor, a swung bar could bleed into the neighbouring tile. The fragment shader would need a `discard` based on the tile-local coordinate.
- **Rig edits.** The rig would live in GLSL, so every change (a new pose joint, the relaxed-arm splay, the kick) means editing shader code, which is harder to debug than JS. The inspector and the portrait, gun and head bakes share this pipeline and would need to keep working.

**Is it worth it?**

All robots together probably cost about 0.5 to 1.5 ms of CPU per frame on the old MacBook. I have not measured that; it is a guess. The instanced version might bring it down to about 0.1 to 0.2 ms. That is a real saving, but it won't change the framerate unless a crowded floor is actually CPU-bound in the `sprites` span.

The first step is a `?perf` dump on the busiest floor. Look at `sprites` against `walk`, `submit` and the vsync gap. If `sprites` is under 1 ms, leave the code as it is. If it is 3 ms or more with a crowd, do the instanced vertex-shader rig. That is the change I'd make, not a Rust port. Send me the dump and I'll read it.

That number only covers the JS and submit side, because headless Chromium's software renderer can't measure GPU time, so your MacBook trace is what will tell us the real gain. `make verify`, `make check-render` and `make check-e2e` all pass, and a fresh server is running on 8080.

## URLs on :8080

- **GPU rig (the new default):** `http://localhost:8080/?floor=5&debug&perf`
- **CPU rig, for the A/B comparison:** `http://localhost:8080/?floor=5&debug&perf&rig=cpu`
- **Trace viewer:** `http://localhost:8080/tools/perf.html`
- **Rig comparison page:** `http://localhost:8080/tools/rig-parity.html?bench=200`

Play a crowded stretch on each of the first two, press **P**, and paste each dump into the trace viewer. Compare the `sprites` span and the `draws` counter between the two. The `?floor=5` in those links is just an example, so use whichever floor has the biggest crowd. The comparison page shows the CPU rig, the GPU rig and the texel diff for every pose, and with `bench=200` it also prints the submit cost per 64-robot batch for both rigs on the machine you open it on.

From another machine, the box's address is `[lan-ip]`.

## What changed

- **Skeleton in the vertex shader** (`robot-core.js`). Each robot is now 16 per-instance floats: its tile, facing, palette index and the `posePlan()` scalars. The pose logic stays in JS. The shader walks each vertex's joint chain, which is at most 5 rotations.
- **All three weapons baked into one mesh.** The mesh holds the body, the bare-hand barrel and every held weapon, tagged by which robots show them. Boxes a robot doesn't show collapse to a single off-screen point: the other weapons, the barrel, or a severed head. That is the same trick `headless` already used, so one fixed mesh serves every loadout.
- **One draw per batch.** The whole batch is one buffer upload and one `drawArraysInstancedANGLE` call, using the `ANGLE_instanced_arrays` extension. Each robot's tile is placed in the shader and clipped by a fragment `discard`, which cuts at exactly the same pixels as the old per-tile scissor.
- **The CPU rig stays as the reference.** It still serves the inspector and the portrait bakes. A batch falls back to it when the instancing extension is missing, or for robots that carry their own camera (`opts.orbit` or `opts.halfV`). Both rigs read one shared table of joint pivots and box sizes, so the only thing mirrored between them is the rotation order per joint chain.
- **`?rig=cpu`** forces the CPU rig in the game, and the `?perf` `draws` counter now counts instanced draws too.

- **Parity test:** `tests/e2e/rig-parity.js` (now part of `make check-render`) renders 160 cases through both rigs in full 64-tile batches and compares the 43-texel tiles. The cases cover every pose and weapon at five animation times, with rotating palettes and facings.
  - **Result:** the two rigs differ by 2 texels in total, both in one kick/machinegun tile, caused by float32 shader trig against float64 JS. The test's budget is 6 texels per tile.
- **Mutation check:** I deliberately broke one joint sign in the shader, and the test failed with 276 differing texels. It catches real regressions.
- **CPU rig unchanged:** the CPU rig's output checksum is identical before and after the refactor (`f8bf295b`). The test script does not pin that checksum by default; set `RIG_GOLDEN=f8bf295b` when running it to enforce it.

## Old vs new, steady-state frames with 4–10 robots

Chrome's timer resolution here is 0.1 ms and I averaged by eye, so these are approximate:

| | Old (CPU rig) | New (GPU rig) |
|---|---|---|
| `draws` | 27 → 40, two per robot | **20, flat whatever the robot count** |
| `sprites` | ~0.3–0.5 ms, frequent spikes of 0.8–2.0 ms | **~0.1–0.2 ms** (absent in some frames, i.e. under 0.1 ms), spikes rare |
| `flush` | ~1.1 ms | ~0.65 ms |
| whole frame (`dur`) | ~1.6 ms | ~1.2 ms |

- The robot pass went from about 0.5 ms to about 0.15 ms and no longer grows with the robot count.
- Most of the 1–2 ms `sprites` spikes are gone.
- The first frame, which pays for shader compiles and sprite bakes, costs about the same in both: `sprites` was 30.2 ms new against 28.5 ms old.

## The CPU is idle either way

Look at the `gap` field in both dumps: it is about 32–34 ms on every frame, which is 30 fps. The engine plus renderer use about 1–1.5 ms of CPU out of each 33 ms. Saving 0.4 ms there cannot change the framerate.

So something else holds it at 30 fps. It is one of two things:

1. **The FPS cap is set to 30.** The default is 120. Check ESC → SETTINGS → FPS CAP, or look at `localStorage['om.fps_cap']`.
2. **The GPU is fill-rate bound and missing every other vsync.** The canvas is 2880×1046, about 3M pixels, and each full-screen layer touches all of them: the backdrop quad, floor and walls, the TV-static quad, plus the scene FBO whenever a post effect is on. A GPU-bound frame shows exactly this pattern: small CPU spans and a gap of about two vsyncs. It would also match the `?aa=1` experience recorded in CLAUDE.md.

The `?perf` trace only measures CPU time, so it can't tell these two apart. It takes about a minute to check by hand:

- Set the FPS cap to uncapped, then look at the HUD FPS or take another dump. If `gap` drops to about 16.7 ms, it was the cap and there is nothing to fix.
- If it stays at about 33 ms, it's the GPU. Then try each of these and watch `gap`:
  - `&noise=0`, which removes one full-screen blended quad.
  - A smaller browser window. Fewer pixels giving a faster frame means fill-rate.
  - `&pixel=3`, which moves the scenery rasterization to art resolution and cuts the full-resolution fill.

If it turns out to be GPU-bound, the next thing I'd build is GPU timing in the `?perf` trace, using `EXT_disjoint_timer_query` where the browser exposes it. Then we'd know which layer costs the most before changing anything.

The rig work is still worth keeping. It takes the robot CPU cost to near zero however many robots are on screen, and it removes the per-robot spikes. It just isn't what stands between you and 60 fps.
I've added the GPU name to the perf dump. I'm making the trace viewer show it, then I'll give you my read of this trace.

The game is GPU-bound, not CPU-bound. The per-frame GPU cost looks too high for what we actually draw, so I doubt it's a plain fill-rate limit of the game's own layers. I need two facts from your machine before I change anything.

## What the trace shows

- **CPU:** about 1 ms per frame, the same as before. With the cap at 120 the frame period is still 29–35 ms, so both the CPU and the cap are ruled out.
- **The period tracks scene content, not vsync.**
  - Stretches with `draws: 16` run at about 29–30 ms per frame.
  - Stretches with `draws: 20` run at about 33–34 ms.
  - A vsync-locked game would show a mix of 16.7 ms and 33.3 ms frames.
  - A steady 29.5 ms means the browser is handing out the next frame at the pace the GPU finishes the previous one.
  - So each frame costs the GPU about 30 ms.
- **That is far too much for this workload.**
  - The batch fragment shader is a single texture fetch times a colour.
  - There are about 20 draws and no post pass.
  - The backdrop and the robots render at art resolution.
  - Even an Intel integrated GPU should finish that at 2880×1046 in well under 10 ms.
- **Your two experiments point the same way.**
  - `pixel=3` rasterizes all of the scenery at art resolution and changed nothing, so floor and wall overdraw is not the cost.
  - `noise=0` removes exactly one full-screen blended quad and you could feel it.
  - A single cheap layer only matters on a GPU that is starved for memory bandwidth or throttled.

## My suspects, most likely first

1. **Chrome is running on the integrated GPU.**
   - If this is a 15" 2018 MacBook Pro, it has a Radeon next to the Intel chip.
   - `powerPreference: "high-performance"` is only a hint, and macOS automatic graphics switching or running on battery can override it.
   - A comment in `renderer.js` already describes this exact symptom: the game crawls at 30 fps on machines that could do 120.
2. **Power throttling.** Chrome's Energy Saver, macOS Low Power Mode, or a hot, clocked-down integrated GPU. Any of these makes every full-screen write expensive.
3. **The canvas presentation path.**
   - `desynchronized: true` is a low-latency hint, and the code comment already tells us to delete it if a platform misbehaves.
   - It's a cheap one-line A/B, but I'd try it after the first two.

## What I need from you

I added the GPU name to the perf dump. It is now in the dump's `meta` and shown in `tools/perf.html`, and it is live on `:8080`.

1. Reload and press **P**. Send me just the `"gpu":"…"` value from the top of the dump; I don't need the frames.
2. Tell me whether you were on battery, and whether Chrome's Energy Saver or macOS Low Power Mode was on.

**Optional check:** halve the browser window's height and see whether the frame period drops roughly in proportion. If it does, the cost scales per pixel, which confirms the bandwidth explanation.

## Depending on the answer

- **Intel GPU and a Radeon exists:** that is the whole story. Turn off automatic graphics switching or plug in. The only code option is cutting the pixel count.
- **Intel is the only GPU:** the real lever is the 3M-pixel backing buffer. I'd add a render-scale option that draws the backing buffer at, say, 1.5× instead of 2× DPR and upscales with NEAREST. That cuts fill by 44%, and the hard-pixel look hides it well. It is a bigger win than shaving individual layers.
- **Already on the Radeon:** something is pathological. I'd build GPU timer queries into `?perf` to find which pass is eating the time.

The small edits to `renderer.js`, `index.html` and `tools/perf.html` are unstaged, like the rest. `check-fmt` passes; I haven't re-run the full `make verify` since them.

I think the probe found it, and I've made a candidate fix. It's a one-line change in how the batch uploads vertices, and I need you to A/B it.

## What the probe says

"Clear only" runs at exactly 16.7 ms, so presenting the canvas is free. Every knockout saves roughly the same 3–7 ms, and two of them don't fit a fill-rate story:

- **Text saves 7 ms.** The HUD text is a few dozen tiny quads. That cannot cost 7 ms of pixels.
- **"No big rects" saved 3 ms while removing nothing.** The report shows `bigRectLayersPerFrame: 0`, so that's the noise floor, which tells you how much to trust each row.

What every knockout has in common is not pixels but **draw calls**. The renderer flushes on every texture switch, and text, robots, the backdrop and the static overlay each add one to three flushes. Take a frame at 33 ms, subtract the 16.7 ms vsync floor and 20 or so flushes, and each flush costs about 1 ms. That is consistent with each flush stalling the pipeline.

## The likely cause

Every flush did `bufferSubData` at offset 0 into one preallocated 2 MiB buffer, `renderer.js:1929`. The previous draw may still be reading that buffer, so the driver has to either wait for it to finish or copy the buffer. On Chrome's ANGLE-Metal path that copy is expensive, and drivers that keep a shadow copy duplicate the whole 2 MiB. Twenty times a frame, that lands squarely in the range the probe measured, and it explains why `pixel=3` did so little: it cut pixels, not flushes.

**The fix** is buffer orphaning: each flush now uploads exactly the vertices it filled through a fresh `bufferData`. The driver hands out a right-sized pooled buffer, and the draws overlap instead of serialising. It is the standard pattern for dynamic vertex data.

## Run the A/B

Both are live on `:8080`:

- **New path (default):** `http://localhost:8080/?floor=5&debug&gpuprobe`
- **Old path (`vbo=sub`):** `http://localhost:8080/?floor=5&debug&gpuprobe&vbo=sub`

Only the baseline row matters. If the new path drops from about 31 ms toward 17, that's it. The other rows should also flatten toward the noise floor, because per-flush cost disappears.

If it only moves a little, the stall is real but not in the buffer, and the next lever is flush count. The main fix there is putting the white pixel that all solid rects sample into the glyph atlas, so rects and text never switch textures. I'd want the A/B numbers before doing that.

## Status

`make verify`, `make check-render` and `make check-e2e` all pass. Everything is unstaged. The `vbo=sub` switch is documented in `docs/URL_PARAMS.md`; I'd remove it once we've settled on the path.

My opinion: the game's own drawing is now only about 6 ms per frame. What keeps you at 52 fps is a fixed cost of about 13 ms that the GPU pays before the game draws anything. I can explain the numbers, but I can't yet say where that 13 ms comes from, so I added probe rows that measure it directly.

## What the two tables say

- **Each full-screen layer costs about 1.8 ms, and the cost is linear.** `+1 blend rect` cost 1.9 ms and `+3 blend rect` cost 5.5 ms. The opaque backdrop costs 1.8 ms and a blended rect costs 1.9 ms, which is why unblending changed nothing.
- **The floor is one layer deep, not several.** `+1 static geo` cost 1.7 ms, the same as a plain rect. My tile-overdraw theory was wrong.
- **`pixel=3` gains nothing, and the data shows why.** It makes the floor and walls cost almost nothing (0.4–0.5 ms), but its composite quad is itself one full-screen layer, so it breaks even. It is an art-direction feature, not a performance one.
- **The budget is already spent before the game draws anything:**

| | ms |
|---|---|
| backdrop | 1.8 |
| floor and walls | 1.7 |
| TV static | 1.9 |
| robots | 0.6 |
| text and everything else | about 0 |
| **the game's drawing** | **about 6** |
| measured frame | 19.4 |
| **unaccounted fixed cost** | **about 13.4** |

With 16.7 ms available and about 13.4 ms already spent, you have room for roughly 1.8 full-screen layers, and you draw three. No amount of tidying our own layers closes a 2.7 ms gap out of 6 ms without removing a layer outright.

## What I think the fixed cost is, unproven

I have two suspects.

- **The macOS display scaler.** A canvas 2880 px wide at DPR 2 means the display is set to "looks like 1440×900".
  - As far as I know, the 2018 Air's panel is 2560×1600. If so, macOS renders the desktop at 2880×1800 and downsamples it to the panel every frame, on the same UHD 617.
  - That would be several layers' worth of work, outside the browser, invisible to us.
- **A browser compositing copy.** If Chrome doesn't promote the canvas to a direct overlay, it copies the canvas into the window once per frame, which costs about one more layer.

## Measuring it

I added two probe rows, `clear +6 rect` and `clear +10 rect`. "Clear only" sits under the vsync floor, so these rows load it with known layers until it rises above the floor. The header now prints the per-layer cost and the fixed cost of presenting the canvas directly. `make verify` passes; I only checked the new rows headless, where the numbers mean nothing but the mechanism works.

Please run `?floor=5&debug&gpuprobe` three times:

1. **As now.** This gives the fixed cost as a measured number.
2. **With the display set to 1280×800** (System Settings → Displays → the "larger text" option), which I believe is an exact 2× of the panel. If the fixed cost drops by several ms, it's the macOS scaler, and nothing in the game can fix that. We would only document it.
3. **With the browser in real fullscreen.** Fullscreen sometimes gets the direct-to-display path, but the canvas also grows, so we'll see which effect wins.

## What I would not do yet

Two options need your decision, so I'm not slipping them in:

- **Clipping the backdrop to where the floor doesn't cover it.** It saves up to 1.8 ms when the floor fills the screen, and nothing on open floors like floor 0. It's worth doing at some point, but it doesn't close the gap alone.
- **The TV static.** It costs 1.9 ms for grain drawn at 7.5% opacity. It could be folded into the batch shader instead of being its own layer, but that changes how the grain sits over blended pixels, which is an art decision.

Fully fullscreen, the canvas is roughly 4.6M pixels, not 3M. Each layer then costs about 2.8 ms, and I'd expect the fixed cost to grow with it. On this GPU at 2× Retina, 60 fps then means at most about one full-screen layer. The three probe runs will show whether that limit is ours to fix or the machine's.

Everything is still unstaged.

Yes, the 13 ms is there even for a plain black screen, and this run confirms it directly. The fixed cost of presenting the canvas measured **13.3 ms**, and each full-screen layer measured 1.79 ms. The two fixed-cost rows fit a straight line: 24.0 ms with 6 rects and 31.2 ms with 10.

## What that means

- Your 60 fps budget is 16.7 ms and 13.3 ms is gone before the game draws anything. That leaves room for about 1.9 full-screen layers. The game draws three, plus the robots.
- At 1.79 ms per 3M pixels, that 13.3 ms is about 22 million pixels of GPU work per frame, inside Chrome or macOS.

I have three suspects for the fixed cost. None is confirmed.

- **How the WebGL context is created.**
  - On macOS an `alpha: false` canvas can make Chrome do extra full-canvas work every frame to emulate a buffer with no alpha channel. That is from memory and not verified here. We chose `alpha: false` hoping it would be cheaper.
  - The `desynchronized` hint is a second variable.
- **Chrome copying the canvas into the window**, if it isn't promoted to a direct overlay.
- **The macOS display scaler**, the "looks like 1440×900" downsample I described last time.

## What I added

I added a `?ctx=` flag that changes one context-creation choice at a time, so the probe's fixed-cost line can be compared against the default. It doesn't replace a full probe run: it changes how the context is created and you run the probe on top of it.

- `ctx=alpha` creates an `alpha: true` context. The blend keeps the canvas alpha at 1, so it stays opaque over the page.
- `ctx=sync` drops the `desynchronized` hint.
- `ctx=lowpower` drops the high-performance GPU request. You have only one GPU, so I expect no effect from this one.

Headless, `ctx=alpha` renders the same picture as the default with no errors. `make verify` and `make check-e2e` pass. I did not re-run `make check-render`. The flags are documented in `docs/URL_PARAMS.md`, and the defaults are unchanged without the flag.

```

?floor=5&debug&gpuprobe&ctx=sync
?floor=5&debug&gpuprobe&ctx=alpha,sync
```

If you can, also run one default probe with the display set to 1280×800. That tests the macOS scaler theory.

## How I'd act on it

- **A `ctx` flag cuts the fixed cost by several ms.** I'd make that the default context. If the gain only shows up in Chrome on macOS, it could be switched on per platform.
- **Only the display mode moves it.** The cost is outside the browser. The game can't fix that and we would document it.
- **Nothing moves it.** About 13 ms is simply what this machine charges for a 3M-pixel canvas at 60 Hz. The remaining options are the two you haven't decided on: clip the backdrop to where the floor doesn't cover it, or fold the TV static into another pass. Those are your call.

## What I changed

- **The default on Apple platforms is now an `alpha: true` context.**
  - The batch blend keeps the canvas alpha at exactly 1.
  - Every full-screen pass already writes alpha 1; I checked all six shaders.
  - The canvas therefore stays opaque over the page and the picture is unchanged.
- **Other platforms keep `alpha: false`.**

- **`?ctx=opaque` forces the old behaviour on a Mac, and `?ctx=alpha` forces the new one anywhere.** That keeps the A/B possible.
- **Docs.** The measured figures and both findings are in CLAUDE.md under the GPU probe section, and the flags are in `docs/URL_PARAMS.md`.

- **Elsewhere I have no measurement.** My guess is the downside is at most one full-screen blend. That is cheap on a desktop GPU, but could matter on something as tight as your MacBook Air.

## 1. The PC experiment

I built a short version of the probe. It takes about 10 to 15 seconds and you don't have to stand still. It reports two numbers: the fixed cost of presenting the canvas and the cost per full-screen layer. Here are the two URLs:

```
?floor=5&gpuprobe=fixed&ctx=opaque      (what non-Apple machines get today)
?floor=5&gpuprobe=fixed&ctx=alpha       (what the Mac now gets)
```

It draws only a clear plus N invisible full-screen rects. It doubles N until the GPU is clearly the limit, so a fast desktop card is measurable too. If even thousands of layers still run at display rate, it says the GPU isn't the limit and gives no fixed cost, so there is nothing to compare on that machine.

The result panel stays hidden while it measures, because an element sitting over the canvas can itself change how the browser presents it. Progress shows in the tab title. The result lands on screen and on the clipboard.

How to read it: compare the "FIXED cost" line between the two runs. If alpha is lower or equal on the PC, I'll make `alpha: true` the default everywhere and delete the platform check. If opaque is clearly lower, the split stays.

I ran it headless with both context kinds. It completes in 13 seconds with no errors, but it runs on software rendering here, so the numbers mean nothing. `make verify` and `make check-e2e` pass; I did not re-run `make check-render` after this change. `localhost:8080` has the new files; your `[deploy-host]` copy needs the updated `tools/gpu-probe.js` and `renderer.js`.

## 2. What the 9.6 ms is

- **What I know.**
  - It is real GPU time. It exists for a bare clear, and the desynchronized hint doesn't change it.
  - 3.6 ms of the original 13.3 was the alpha emulation, now gone.
  - At about 1.8 ms per 3M pixels, the remaining 9.6 ms is roughly 16M pixels of work per frame that isn't ours.
- **What I don't know.** Who spends it. I have two suspects.
  - Chrome copying the canvas into the window's surface instead of handing it straight to the display.
  - The macOS scaled display mode. macOS composites a 2880×1800 desktop and downsamples it to the panel every frame, on this same GPU.

Three quick-probe runs would split them:

| Run | If the fixed cost… | Then it's… |
|---|---|---|
| Same URL, window half as tall | roughly halves | per canvas pixel, so the browser side, which we might influence |
| | barely moves | per display, so macOS, outside the game's reach |
| Display set to 1280×800 | drops several ms | the macOS scaler, which we'd document rather than fix |
| Safari, same URL | is very different | specific to Chrome's presentation path |

I can't promise a gain until we know which one it is. If it turns out to be Chrome's copy, the two things I'd look at are whether the canvas qualifies for direct presentation and whether any other page element is forcing a composite.

## 3. One shot for the three layers

Yes, there is a strategy. It's tricky, but I think it's tractable, and if it works as I expect it's exact, with no visual compromise.

- **Backdrop and floor.**
  - They never both show at the same pixel: the floor covers the backdrop wherever the level is.
  - Draw the backdrop only outside the floor's on-screen rectangle, as strips around it, and the two become one layer's worth of pixels.
  - It saves up to 1.8 ms when the floor fills the screen, and nothing on open floors like floor 0.
  - The catch is the camera roll, so the excluded rectangle has to be slightly inset.
- **The TV static.** Fold it into the batch shader: every fragment adds the grain for its screen position, and the separate full-screen quad disappears.
  - The grain is an affine function of colour. Blending two grained colours gives exactly the grain of the blended colour, so by my algebra the final pixels should match today's. I haven't tested that yet.
  - The cost is one extra texture fetch per fragment, which is far less than a full layer.
- **The tricky parts.**
  - Pixel groups must not be grained on the inside, and they need the premultiplied form of the grain on their composite quad.
  - Frames with a post effect have to keep the grain at the very end.
  - The backdrop strips have to get their texture coordinates right.
- **How I'd test it.** Headless pixel diff. Render one frozen frame the old way and the new way, and require every pixel to be identical.

Expected result on your MacBook Air: the layers drop from about 5.4 ms to about 2 ms. The frame goes from about 15.6 ms to about 12 ms, which is about 4.5 ms of headroom without touching the fixed cost.

Do you want me to build it? I'd do the grain fold first. It always pays, and it is the part I expect to be exact. The backdrop clip comes second, because it only pays where the floor covers the screen.

## 1. The PC numbers

## 2. What I found on the Mac's 9.6 ms

I found nothing that would let us accelerate it. There is no flag or trick that lowers it.

- **The alpha cost is documented.** MDN's WebGL best-practices page says browsers emulate alpha-less buffers on some platforms, and that masking the alpha channel has fairly high overhead. That matches the 3.6 ms we removed.
- **Chrome already takes the good path on macOS.** A Chromium design note says the WebGL drawing buffer is backed by an IOSurface, which is the macOS shared GPU surface. That surface goes straight to CoreAnimation, and the design was adopted to avoid the framebuffer copy the earlier path needed.
  - So my "extra copy into the window" suspect is weaker than I made it sound.
- **Scaled display modes cost real GPU work.** macOS writeups describe it rendering at twice the chosen "looks like" size and downsampling to the panel every frame. They recommend native modes on Intel Macs and thermally limited MacBook Airs.
- **Yes, other canvases hit this too.** Several threads report canvas and WebGL performance that is much worse on Retina MacBook panels than on external monitors.
  - Any full-window 60 fps canvas on that machine pays a similar toll. It isn't specific to your game.
  - I agree it's a poor state of affairs, but it sits below the browser's API surface.

The 1280×800 display-mode run would still tell you how much of the 9.6 ms is the scaler. It would be for your information only, because the game can't change the result.

## 3. The grain fold

- **What changed.**
  - The TV static is no longer its own full-screen layer.
  - The batch shader grains every fragment as it lands on the canvas, looking up the same noise by screen position.
- **What is skipped or handled specially.**
  - Pixel groups are skipped on the inside.
  - Their composite quad uses the premultiplied form.
  - The end-of-frame quad is still used when the frame doesn't open with a backdrop, or when a post pass follows. That covers the title screen and the menus.
- **Pixel diff.** The new `tests/e2e/grain-fold.js` captures a live game frame, freezes the game, and renders that one stream three ways with a fixed noise roll: the old quad, the fold, and no grain.

| Scene | max channel delta | pixels off by more than 1 | grain strength, fold vs quad |
|---|---|---|---|
| gameplay | 2 | 0.000% | 3.83 vs 3.82 |
| `pixel=3` world | 2 | 0.000% | 3.77 vs 3.77 |
| floor 0 dialogue (slab, text, portraits) | 2 | 0.049% | 3.96 vs 3.92 |

- **Why it isn't bit-exact.** The leftover difference is 8-bit rounding. The quad rounds the finished colour once, and the fold rounds at every blend. By my algebra the pixels are otherwise identical.
- **Why "no grain" is in the test.** The test compares against a no-grain render so a fold that silently switched itself off could not pass.
- **A/B switch.** `?grain=quad` forces the old path.

- **What comes next.** The backdrop clip is the remaining piece of the one-shot plan, if you want it after seeing this.

The "device pixel ratio" is the number of real screen pixels inside one CSS pixel. The advice is to stop matching it and render the game at the CSS size instead.

## The two kinds of pixel

The browser measures the page in CSS pixels. Your game window is 1440 × 523 of them. On a Retina screen, macOS and the browser pack 2 × 2 real screen pixels into each CSS pixel so that text looks sharp. That factor is `window.devicePixelRatio`, and on your MacBook Air it is 2.

A `<canvas>` has two separate sizes:

- **Display size.** This is how much of the page it covers, in CSS pixels: 1440 × 523.
- **Backing buffer.** This is how many pixels the GPU actually renders into. The game sets it, and it can be any size.

If the two sizes differ, the browser stretches the buffer to fit the display size.

## What the game does now

The game sets the backing buffer to the CSS size multiplied by the ratio: 1440 × 2 by 523 × 2, which is 2880 × 1046, about 3M pixels. `Graphics::sync_size` does this. It is why your probe reports `canvas 2880x1046 (dpr 2)`. Every rendered pixel lands on exactly one real screen pixel, which is the sharpest picture possible. The cost is that each full-screen layer has to fill 3M pixels.

## What "clamp to 1.0" means

Ignore the ratio and make the backing buffer 1440 × 523, about 0.75M pixels. The browser then stretches that image over the same area, and each rendered pixel covers a 2 × 2 block of real screen pixels.

| | Buffer | Pixels | Cost of one full-screen layer on your MacBook Air |
|---|---|---|---|
| Now (ratio 2) | 2880 × 1046 | about 3.0M | about 1.8 ms |
| Clamped (ratio 1) | 1440 × 523 | about 0.75M | about 0.45 ms |

- **Everything that scales with pixel count gets about 4× cheaper.** That covers our layers, and probably a good part of the 9.6 ms the browser and macOS spend presenting the canvas.
- **The per-layer figure is an estimate, not a measurement.** I got it by dividing by four.
- **The gain matters most in fullscreen.** At ratio 2, fullscreen is about 4.6M pixels, where your window is 3M.

## What it costs visually

The game is rendered at half the linear resolution and then enlarged:

- **Art.**
  - Robot, prop and floor art is already chunky. A robot's art pixel is roughly 3 CSS pixels wide, so it still lands on whole rendered pixels.
  - The art would look much the same.
- **Hard edges.**
  - Rotated walls, the camera sway and sprite outlines would step twice as coarsely. A staircase that was 1 real pixel per step becomes 2.
- **Text.**
  - VT323 HUD text gets chunkier.
- **Motion.**
  - Things move in steps of one rendered pixel, which is now 2 real pixels. Motion is a little less smooth.
- **How the browser stretches the image.**
  - Left alone, the browser stretches with smoothing, which blurs everything. That would go against your art direction.
  - With the CSS rule `image-rendering: pixelated` it uses nearest-neighbour, so each pixel becomes a crisp 2 × 2 block.
  - Exactly 1.0 on a 2× screen is a clean integer scale.
  - A value in between, such as 1.5, can't stay crisp: either it blurs or the pixel blocks come out uneven.

## Why the summary mentions fullscreen

That is where pixel count jumps. Some games render at full ratio in a window and switch to the clamped size only in fullscreen. Others lower the resolution automatically when the framerate drops.

So the clamp is a trade of sharpness for speed. It isn't a bug fix. It was right to refuse it while we still had real bugs to find. With those fixed, it is the one remaining change that alters the pixel count itself.

- **The correction.** I said every rendered pixel lands on exactly one real screen pixel. In this display mode that is false.
  - Your 2880-wide canvas is resampled down to about 2560 physical pixels by macOS, with filtering.
  - The hard NEAREST edges you care about are already being softened slightly by the OS, after the browser is done. Neither the game nor Chrome can see that or stop it.

## Does it explain the cost?

Partly, I think. The scaled mode means two things:

- Everything on screen is rendered at 5.2M pixels instead of the panel's 4.1M.
- A full-frame downsample pass runs on top of that, 60 times a second, on the same GPU.

That is a plausible chunk of the 9.6 ms fixed cost, but it is unmeasured. It is still my leading suspect for a large part of it.

## Can you tell Chrome or macOS to use real pixels for the canvas?

No, not as far as I know.

- **From a web page.** I know of no web API for it. The Fullscreen API does not change the display mode either.
- **From macOS.** It does not offer per-window opt-out for ordinary windowed apps, native ones included.
- **Rendering the canvas at 1.78× ourselves would be worse.** Chrome would stretch it to 2×, then macOS would shrink it again, so it would be resampled twice.

What does work is on the user's side. Set the display to 1280 × 800, which is the "larger text" option.

- **1:1 pixels.** That is exactly half the panel, so macOS renders at 2560 × 1600 and sends it to the glass unscaled.
- **Crisp edges.** A canvas pixel then really is one physical pixel, and NEAREST edges stay hard.
- **Less work for the GPU.** For the same physical window there are about 21% fewer pixels to fill, and the scaler pass disappears.

## Measuring it

Two quick runs of about 15 seconds each. Keep the same physical window size for both:

```
?floor=5&gpuprobe=fixed        in the current mode (looks like 1440×900)
?floor=5&gpuprobe=fixed        after switching the display to 1280×800
```

Compare the "FIXED cost" line between the two runs. The difference is what the scaled mode costs on your MacBook Air.

## What this changes for the game

- **Detection.** The game cannot detect this mode. The ratio reads 2 either way.
  - `screen.width` gives the "looks like" size, not the panel.
  - All we could do is document it, with wording like "for the sharpest picture and best framerate on a MacBook, use a native 2× display mode".
- **The clamp, worse.** It weakens my case for the ratio-1 clamp on this machine.
  - In your current mode, a ratio-1 canvas pixel would cover about 1.78 physical pixels, not a clean 2 × 2 block.
  - It would come out slightly uneven and soft.
  - The clean integer scaling I described only holds in a native 2× mode.
- **The clamp, better.** It also makes the full 2× render slightly less valuable than I claimed. About 11% of that linear resolution is thrown away by the scaler before it reaches the glass.

The quick probe's numbers and the full probe's numbers can't be compared with each other, because they measure your GPU under different amounts of load. That is why the quick probe looks better than the earlier 1440 × 900 result.

## Why the two probes disagree

Both probes draw a clear plus N invisible full-screen rects and fit a straight line through the results. Both results below were taken on the same canvas in the same display mode.

| Probe | N | Cost per layer | Fixed cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full probe | 6 and 10 | 1.82 ms | 9.6 ms |
| Quick probe | 32 and 64 | 1.06 ms | 4.3 ms |

A GPU running at one speed would give the same line both times. Putting the two sets of points together, the curve is not straight:

- From 6 to 10 rects, each extra rect costs 1.82 ms.
- From 10 to 32 rects, each extra rect costs only about 0.47 ms.
- From 32 to 64 rects, each extra rect costs 1.06 ms.

My best explanation is clock scaling. At gameplay-level load the UHD 617 idles at a low clock, and under sustained heavy load it speeds up. I haven't verified this.

If that's right, neither "fixed cost" is the true one. Each is the intercept of a line fitted at a different GPU speed. The figure that matters for the game is the one measured at gameplay load, which is 9.6 ms. Calling it a fixed cost was too strong on my part. It is an extrapolation that depends on the load it was measured at.

## Your actual question: 1440 × 900 vs 1280 × 800

These are both quick-probe runs, so they can be compared directly.

| | Canvas | Per layer | Per million pixels | Fixed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| looks like 1440 × 900 | 2880 × 1046 (3.01M px) | 1.056 ms | 0.351 ms | 4.29 ms |
| 1280 × 800 | 2560 × 846 (2.17M px) | 0.759 ms | 0.350 ms | 3.56 ms |

- **Layer cost depends on pixel count alone.** It is 0.35 ms per million pixels in both modes, identical to three digits. The scaled mode does not make drawing slower per pixel.
- **The fixed cost fell by about 17%.** That is roughly in line with the drop in pixel count. There is no sign of a large separate macOS scaler pass, so that suspect from earlier is mostly cleared.
- **The scaled mode still costs you.** It makes everything about 27% more pixels, and its resampling softens your hard edges. It just doesn't add an expensive extra step.
- **Practical upshot.** 1280 × 800 gives you crisper pixels, because the mapping is truly 1:1, and about 20–25% less GPU work for the same physical window. It is a user setting, so at most it goes in the documentation.

## To see the curve directly

I added a third probe mode that walks a ladder of N from 0 to 64 and prints the cost of each step:

```
?floor=5&gpuprobe=curve        (~35 s, no need to stand still)
```

If the clock-scaling idea is right, the step cost will drop sharply somewhere past N = 10. The run will also show where gameplay sits on that curve.

I can't do anything about the GPU's clock from a web page. Knowing where the knee is would still tell us how much headroom the 60 fps margin really has.

I checked the new mode headless: it completes with no errors, but it runs on software rendering, so the numbers mean nothing. `make verify` passes. Everything is unstaged. Your `[deploy-host]` copy needs the updated `tools/gpu-probe.js`.

I was wrong about clock scaling, and the curve run disproves it. The difference between the probe modes was the probe's own result panel.

## What the curve shows

- **Hidden panel:**
  - Up to 12 extra full-screen layers still fit inside the 16.7 ms frame.
  - Beyond that the line is straight at 1.06 ms per layer.

- **Full probe:**
  - The clear plus 6 rects read 20.5 ms and the clear plus 10 rects read 27.8 ms.
  - During those runs the result panel was visible over the canvas.
- **Conclusion:** the only difference between the two runs is the panel, so it is the probe's own observer effect.
- **Mechanism, inferred and not proven:**
  - An HTML element over the canvas makes Chrome present the canvas a more expensive way.
  - On your MacBook Air it roughly doubled every number I measured:

| | With the panel | Without the panel |
|---|---|---|
| bare clear | about 9.6 ms | about 4.5 ms |
| one full-screen layer | about 1.8 ms | about 1.06 ms |

I hid the panel in the quick probe as a precaution for this reason, but I underestimated how much it matters.

## What this means for earlier results

- **The A/B verdicts stand.**
  - The batch upload fix, the `alpha: true` context and the backdrop clip were all judged against runs taken the same way.
  - The grain fold being a loss was judged the same way too.
- **The absolute numbers I quoted were about twice too high for the real game**, because nothing sits over its canvas during play. That covers the "9.6 ms fixed cost", "1.8 ms per layer" and "only 1 ms of headroom".
- **Rough estimate for normal play:**
  - About 4.5 ms for the clear, three layers at 1.06 ms each and the robots come to about 8–9 ms of the 16.7 ms budget.
  - I have not measured that on the real frame yet.
- **The fullscreen forecast is off.**
  - I said about 45 fps, and that also used the inflated numbers.
  - A rough estimate now lands around 13 ms, so probably still 60 fps.

## What I changed

- **Every probe mode now hides its panel while measuring.**
  - Progress shows in the tab title, and the table appears at the end.
  - Full-probe numbers will now be trustworthy in absolute terms.
- **New mode `?gpuprobe=headroom`.**
  - It keeps the real game frame and adds N invisible layers on top.
  - It shows how many extra layers the scene can take before dropping below 60 fps.
  - It also reads the frame's actual GPU time off the fitted line.
- **Docs.**

  - They now say to never leave a DOM element over the game canvas during play.

This settles it. The performance problem on your MacBook Air is fixed, and the machine has plenty of headroom.

## What this run says

- **Canvas size.** This run was on a 2880 × 1430 canvas, 4.12M pixels. That is close to fullscreen and 37% more pixels than any earlier probe.
- **Frame cost.** The real game frame costs 8.6 ms of GPU time against a 16.7 ms budget.
- **Headroom.** That leaves about 8 ms, or 5 to 6 extra full-screen layers, before the game would drop below 60 fps. The earlier "1 ms of headroom" figure was inflated by the probe's own panel.
- **Consistency.** The cost per layer is 1.44 ms here, which is 0.35 ms per million pixels. That is the same figure as your quick-probe runs in both display modes. The cost of a layer depends on its pixel count and nothing else.

Fullscreen at 2× holds 60 fps with room to spare. The kill flash, a post effect or the pause-menu static each add about one layer, so they fit.

The clamp and render-scale question is closed. The game doesn't need it on this machine.

## What got it from 30 fps to here

| Change | Effect |
|---|---|
| Batch upload: right-sized `bufferData` per flush instead of `bufferSubData` into a busy 2 MiB buffer | The main fix. Your first traces showed a real 30 fps, and those were taken without the probe panel. |
| `alpha: true` context on Apple platforms (measured worse on your PC, so opaque stays elsewhere) | About 3.6 ms per frame, measured while the probe panel was visible, so the real saving is likely smaller. |
| Backdrop drawn only where the floor doesn't cover it | Small gain, scene-dependent, can't cost anything. |
| GPU rig for the robots | No framerate gain here. Robot cost stays flat however many are on screen. |
| Grain fold | Measured a loss, kept behind `?grain=fold`. |

One lesson is worth keeping, and it is already in CLAUDE.md. An HTML element over the canvas roughly doubles the presentation cost on this machine. Nothing should ever sit over the game canvas during play.

## What I'd do now

- **Stop optimizing.** Nothing left is worth it on this evidence.
- **Optional re-test of the grain fold.**
  - Run the same URL with `&grain=fold` and compare the headroom line. It was judged while the panel was visible.
  - I still expect it to be a loss, and with 8 ms spare it no longer matters either way.
- **A/B flags.**
  - `?vbo=sub`, `?ctx=`, `?backdrop=full` and `?grain=fold` are inert without their flag.
  - I'm leaving them in so a future regression can be bisected on real hardware in a minute.
  - Tell me if you'd rather strip any of them.

## State of the tree

Everything is unstaged for your sync.

- **`make verify`:** passed on the final code.
- **`make check-render` and `make check-e2e`:** last passed when the backdrop clip went in. Since then only `tools/gpu-probe.js` and the docs have changed.

With this clean measurement, the grain fold is a trade-off and not the clear loss I reported earlier. I've corrected the docs, and the fold stays off by default.

## The two headroom runs side by side

Both used the same 4.12 Mpx canvas with the probe panel hidden.

| | Default (quad) | `grain=fold` |
|---|---|---|
| GPU time of the game frame | 8.6 ms | **6.8 ms** |
| cost of one extra full-screen layer | **1.44 ms** | 2.11 ms |
| extra layers before dropping under 60 fps | **5.6** (first dip at N = 8) | 4.7 (first dip at N = 6) |
| headroom in ms | 8.0 ms | **9.9 ms** |

- **What the fold gains.** It removes the static's own layer, so today's frame gets about 1.8 ms cheaper.
- **What the fold costs.** Its extra texture fetch makes every batch fragment about 47% more expensive. Each additional layer costs more, and the frame tolerates fewer of them.
- **Break-even.** By my arithmetic from these figures, the two come out even at roughly 2 full-screen layers of batch fill per frame. Today's scenes sit under that, so the fold wins. A busier scene would lose.
- **Why the earlier verdict was wrong.** I had reported fragments costing twice as much and a 1.5 ms net loss. That was measured with the probe panel over the canvas. It was the observer effect again, and that verdict is void.

## Why it stays off by default

- **It's within the noise.**
  - Both frames sit far under the 16.7 ms budget, so the fold buys nothing you can see.
  - The 1.8 ms gain is within the error of an extrapolated intercept.
- **The plain shader scales better.** Per-layer cost is what bites when a scene gets heavier. That means more translucent UI, a flash or bigger effects, and that is exactly when you need the margin.
- **It's simpler.** One fetch, no special cases for pixel groups or post-effect frames.

This is a judgment call and not a measurement outcome, so it's yours to overrule. `?grain=fold` stays available, the pixel-diff test keeps it correct, and flipping the default is a one-line change.

## What I updated

- **Docs corrected.** The earlier "measured a loss" text was no longer true. I replaced it with the trade-off above in four places: the shader comment in `renderer.js`, CLAUDE.md, `docs/URL_PARAMS.md` and the test header.
- **Earlier verdict recorded as void.** The docs note that the earlier figures were taken with the panel visible.
- **Checks.** `make verify` and `make check-render` pass. I didn't re-run `make check-e2e`. The only `renderer.js` change since it last passed is this comment.

Everything is unstaged.

I'd still stop optimizing here. The game runs at 60 fps near fullscreen on the MacBook Air with about half the frame budget free.
